paper_title: CLIFT: Conformal Self-Verification for Web Agent Training and Test-Time Scaling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Open-source web agents are now strong enough to execute realistic browser tasks, but training them with reinforcement learning still depends on weak supervision: binary task success is too sparse for credit assignment, while frontier-language-model judges are too expensive to call at every step and cannot be assumed available at deployment. We introduce CLIFT, a training and test-time scaling method built around conformal self-verification. During training, the agent answers natural-language verification questions about its own rollouts; a Compositional Conformal Certifier keeps only question signals whose URL-conditional evidence agrees with a training-time judge, assigns signed trust weights through polarity-aware lift, and blends the resulting verifier score into per-step rewards in a way that never subtracts from the judge baseline. At test time, the same certified bank is frozen and reused as structured evidence for Conformal Trajectory Selection (CTS): the agent samples a greedy rollout and one or more diverse retries, the self-verifier summarises each URL trace, and a conservative majority-vote rule chooses whether to swap away from the current incumbent without calling any external judge. This single mechanism supports three settings. On WebArena Infinity, CLIFT achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source web agents. On VisualWebArena, a bank trained with the open model transfers to GPT-5.5 at test time and reaches state-of-the-art performance under the canonical harness. On Online Mind2Web, without training an agent on the benchmark, translating the certified question bank improves a live-web agent in zero-shot evaluation. Together these results position conformal self-verification as a way to turn costly judge feedback into a reusable training signal and a judge-free test-time scaling signal.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Open-source web agents have reached the point where they can operate realistic browser interfaces, but the verifier remains the bottleneck for improving them with reinforcement learning. binary success signal is easy to deploy but too sparse for credit assignment: when all rollouts in GRPO group [Shao et al., 2024] receive the same outcome, the advantage estimate collapses. frontier language model judge [Bai et al., 2022, Liu et al., 2023] provides richer feedback, but it is costly during training and cannot be assumed available at test time. This tension is especially visible in web-agent benchmarks: WAI [Zhou, 2026] uses programmatic per-app verifiers, VWA [Koh et al., 2024] uses outcome-based URL/DOM checks, and live-web suites such as OM2W [Xue et al., 2025] depend on noisy LLM judges. The policy is often not the only limiting object; the way we score and select its rollouts can dominate the observed success rate. CLIFT asks whether the judges feedback can be turned into reusable verifier that the agent carries with itself, rather than separate process reward model [Lightman et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2024] or post-hoc best-of-N scorer [Cobbe et al., 2021, Snell et al., 2025]. CLIFT maintains bank of natural-language verification questions about web-agent behaviour and certifies which questions Preprint. Table 1: Feedback mechanisms for web-agent RL and test-time scaling. Dense = step-level feedback beyond binary outcome; URL = URL-state grounding; Cert. = certified trust; J-free = judge-free test time; TTS = test-time scaling; Xfer = reusable bank transfer. Approach Outcome RLVR / GRPO (trajectory outcome) [Shao et al., 2024] Stratified GRPO (structural strata) [Zhu et al., 2025] Rich-feedback self-distillation (teacher feedback) [Hübotter et al., 2026] Process / verifier reward models (learned PRM) [Lightman et al., 2024] Post-hoc search / BoN (sample then select) [Snell et al., 2025] Conformal routing / judging (uncertainty gate) [Badshah et al., 2026] CLIFT (URL-certified bank for training and CTS) Dense URL Cert. J-free TTS Xfer are reliable at which URL states. The same bank is used in two places (Figure 2). During training, certified bank evidence is blended with the comparative judge to produce denser per-step reward and URL-stratified advantages. At test time, the trained agent runs greedy trajectory plus diverse retries; the frozen certified bank summarizes each URL trace; and conservative trajectory selector keeps one emitted trajectory per task. The common object is not new model but calibrated verifier: set of questions, URL scopes, polarity signs, and conformal trust weights that can be reused after training. The certifier is the part that makes this more than prompt engineering. Each verification question carries URL scope and polarity sign indicating whether YES is evidence of progress or failure. Mondrian adaptive conformal tracker [Gibbs and Candès, 2021, Vovk, 2012] estimates whether that question separates highand lowjudge rollouts at the relevant URL granularity. Certified questions receive signed trust weights. During training this gives verifier reward that can only add evidence on top of the judge baseline, preventing the reward-collapse failure of earlier linear blends. During test-time scaling, the same signed evidence is frozen and presented to comparative selector over two completed trajectories. In both cases, the question bank is compact interface between expensive judge feedback and the agents own rollouts. Figure 1: CLIFT concept. Vanilla GRPO broadcasts one trajectory-scalar reward; CLIFT scores each visited URL with verification questions and inherits the URL score to actions taken there. Full pipeline: Figure 2. We evaluate this idea in three complementary ways. On WAI, where programmatic verifiers provide dense training supervision, CLIFT improves trainable open Gemma-4 agent and reaches the strongest public 9-app score we are aware of; the point is both training and CTS on the same open backbone. On VWA, where the evaluation is more outcome-based, we use the bank created during Gemma-4 training as test-time verifier for GPT-5.5, showing that the learned verification knowledge transfers to stronger closed backbone and reaches state-of-the-art performance under the canonical harness. On OM2W, we push transfer further: no agent is trained on OM2W; instead, the certified question bank is translated and recalibrated, then used by CTS to improve live-web test-time scaling. These three stories support the same claim: conformal self-verification is useful both as training signal and as reusable, judge-free test-time scaling signal. Related work is discussed after the empirical section (6).

sections.title: 3 Experimental Design
sections.content: We evaluate CLIFT as both training method and test-time scaling method. Table 2: Experimental roles. OM2W supplies no reported policy-training data. WAI is the primary training setting: its selfhosted SaaS-style apps expose programmatic verifiers that can support online RL and publicboard comparison. VWA is the controlled transfer setting: its Reddit, Shopping, and Classifieds environments use outcome-based URL/DOM checks, so we test whether bank learned while training an open model remains useful when applied to GPT-5.5 at inference. OM2W is the live-web transfer setting: it contains 300 public-domain tasks judged by an LLM rubric, and no reported policy is trained on OM2W data. in-domain + board transfer to GPT-5.5 zero-shot transfer train Gemma-4 train bank none WAI VWA OM2W Training role Benchmark Eval role 3.1 Task synthesis and bank construction Training tasks are synthesized without reading evaluation tasks. WAI seeds come from app descriptions; VWA seeds come from SynthAgent [Wang et al., 2026] site exploration. Two frontier LLMs expand the seeds, and shared filter removes malformed, duplicate, hardcoded, pure-lookup, and trivial-navigation tasks. The reported checkpoint trains on 1,886 WAI tasks and 1,272 VWA tasks across 16 LoRA shards. OM2W is excluded from policy training and used only for bank transfer and CTS. Appendix A.2 gives CLIFT training details. 3.2 Per-benchmark protocols The three benchmarks probe complementary properties of the same verifier bank: WAI tests whether certified self-verification can train stronger open agent, VWA tests whether the trained-on-open bank transfers to frozen closed backbone, and OM2W tests whether the same bank recalibrates for live-web zero-shot selection. WAI. We train Gemma 4 31B + LoRA with the full URL-path / host / global CCC hierarchy. The comparison isolates three effects: the base browser-use backbone, vanilla GRPO with the same comparative judge but no certified bank, and CLIFT with certified step-level feedback. We then apply CTS to the trained checkpoint to measure whether the frozen bank gives an additional no-regression test-time selection gain on the same in-domain tasks. VWA. We use the bank learned during open-model training as structured evidence for stronger closed backbone. GPT-5.5 is not updated and sees the same completed-task interface; the only added component is CTS over finished trajectories. This setting isolates whether the bank stores transferable web-interaction knowledge rather than merely improving the Gemma-4 policy that produced it. OM2W. We translate and recalibrate the WAI/VWA bank for live-web domains, then run CTS directly at inference. Reported rows use upstream Gemma-4 or GPT-5.5 weights with no OM2Wspecific LoRA. Question translation rewrites benchmark-specific URL patterns into the live-web equivalents, drops predicates that no longer apply, and adds OM2W-specific failure-mode questions for bot-block pages, hallucinated extraction, partial-filter application, and wrong-final-answer stops. The recalibration pass scores each translated or new question on held-out OM2W rollout sample using the same lift-based certifier as training, so any reported gain comes from cross-benchmark transfer of the certified question taxonomy plus the calibration recipe, not from policy training on OM2W. 5 Table 3: WAI leaderboard slice. Success rates on the public 9-app comparison set; values are percentages without percent signs. The CLIFT +CTS column reports the trained Gemma-4 backbone with K=3 Conformal Trajectory Selection (one selected trajectory per task). Overall is the taskweighted success rate over the 9 apps and matches the CLIFT +CTS row of Table 6. WAI asks whether certified self-verification improves an open trainable web agent; VWA asks whether the bank learned during open-model training remains useful for stronger closed model; OM2W asks whether the same bank can be translated and recalibrated for live-web zero-shot selection. 4.1 Training with certified feedback The public-board comparison in Table 3 is the main WAI headline: CLIFT-trained Gemma-4 with K=3 CTS reaches the highest 9-app success rate among the published systems we compare against (Claude Opus 4.6 is the trainingtime judge; CTS itself calls no external judge). The gain is not concentrated in one easy app: CLIFT wins 7 of 9 apps, is competitive on the rest, and improves the same Gemma-4 browseruse backbone by 12.8 percentage points overall. The two apps led by Gemini 3 Flash are within the leaderboards integer-rounding noise, and the larger 110-task Gmail variant is reported separately in Figure 4. This is the in-domain training claim: the verifier bank is not merely post-hoc reranker; it changes the online RL trajectory enough for 31B open model to exceed the public frontier reference on the matched WAI slice. Figure 3: WAI training reward. CLIFT separates from vanilla GRPO under the same judge and browser-use stack. Figure 4: WAI progression and gains. Operating points and deltas. The training trace in Figure 3 explains why the gap is not just larger rollout budget at evaluation time. Once the certified bank begins contributing signed per-step evidence, training separates from vanilla GRPO before selection is ever used. This lets the WAI story read from training dynamics to aggregate success, rather than from single final leaderboard number alone. The reward curves also make the role of CTS easier to interpret: the selector is operating on an already-improved policy, so small additional WAI lift is expected rather than failure of test-time scaling. For the aggregate comparison, Figure 4 keeps the operating points in order: base Gemma-4, vanilla GRPO, corrected Opus 4.6, CLIFT, and final CLIFT +CTS. The same-denominator claim is no per-app regression, so the CTS bar marks the final conservative 6 selection point rather than pure reranking lift. Training supplies the large WAI jump, CTS preserves it and adds small safe lift, and the larger test-time-scaling effects appear below. 4.2 Bank transfer to closed backbone Table 4: VWA success rates. VWA is the controlled transfer benchmark between the two training settings. Its three Docker environments have deterministic URL/DOM outcome verifiers, but their visual grounding, page layouts, and navigation routines differ from WAIs SaaS apps. We therefore use VWA to ask whether bank learned while training an open Gemma-4 agent can still provide useful evidence when the evaluated policy is GPT5.5, the executor weights are frozen, and only the certified question bank is reused at inference. The published baselines in Table 4 follow the VisualWebArena comparison protocol [Koh et al., 2024]; lower published baselines are omitted from the Table 4 follows the same accounting convention as the OM2W table: each selected-output row emits exactly one trajectory per task, so it is directly comparable to the base rollout on the same task set. The Gemma rows isolate the training effect on an open backbone: CLIFT improves the base model before any closed-model transfer is introduced, and CTS adds smaller additional lift. This mirrors the WAI pattern, but at lower absolute success rates because VWAs visual and navigation demands are less aligned with the training harness. The GPT-5.5 rows test the transfer claim directly. The policy weights are unchanged; only the certified bank evidence and CTS selection are added at inference. Adding CTS with rollout budget K=4 raises the weighted average to 53.7, narrowly above WALTs 52.9 reference, with gains on all three environments. The strongest message is not that VWA is solved (the human row remains far above every agent) but that bank constructed while training an open model remains useful when the underlying executor is closed model. 4.3 Cross-benchmark transfer Table 5: Transferred bank on OM2W. Questions are reused from WAI/VWA or expanded, then recalibrated on OM2W rollouts; the final certified bank has 75 positive-lift and 25 negative-lift questions with mean lift 0.34. OM2W is our hardest setting: 300 liveweb tasks across roughly 30 public domains, judged end-to-end by an LLM rubric rather than DOM matching. We use it as pure transfer benchmark: no reported policy is finetuned on OM2W data. The only adaptation is at the verifier layer: questions mined from the WAI/VWA banks are filtered, rewritten, expanded for live-web failure modes, and recalibrated on OM2W rollouts. Table 5 compresses the main bank evidence. The transferred taxonomy does not collapse under the noisier liveweb judge; instead, 100 of 132 questions certify, including both positive progress signals and negative failure-mode signals. This is the strongest evidence that the bank is reusable artifact rather than benchmark-local prompt list. WAI bank VWA bank OM2W expansion keep/rewrite keep/rewrite live-web checks 33 (91.7%) 31 (64.6%) 36 (75.0%) Construction 100 (75.8%) Final bank 36 48 48 Certified 132 qs Origin 132 Figure 5 reports realised success: every + ours row emits one selected trajectory per task, not an oracle union over samples. On the open backbone, the transferred bank and CTS raise Gemma-4 from 40.0 to 45.0, enough to exceed the GPT-5.5 low-effort baseline on the same judge (43.7). On the stronger GPT-5.5 high-effort backbone, the same test-time mechanism raises success from 49.7 to 61.0 at rollout budget K=4, +11.3pp gain. This is where test-time scaling is most visible: unlike WAI, where training already moves the greedy policy close to its ceiling, OM2W leaves substantial 7 room for the selector to choose among distinct completed trajectories. The same numbers also show that the open Gemma-4 backbone with transferred selection reaches 45.0, slightly above the GPT-5.5 low-effort baseline, even though no OM2W policy weights are trained. The cross-benchmark result also clarifies what transfers. The policy does not: the Gemma rows use upstream weights and the GPT-5.5 rows keep the closed model fixed. What transfers is the certified question taxonomy plus the calibration recipe, which turns prior judge feedback into structured evidence for new live-web environment. Because the bank is just list of URL-scoped, polarity-tagged questions with calibrated trust weights, recalibration on new domain only requires sample of judge-scored rollouts; no policy update is needed to begin selecting trajectories. Detailed bank construction and transfer tables are in Appendix A.4. Figure 5: OM2W transfer gains. Realised SR; is rollout budget. 4.4 Ablation study Table 6: WAI ablation summary. Success rates are shown without percent signs. All training rows use Claude Opus 4.6 as the comparative judge with the same browser-use backbone; only the bank/CTS components vary. Steps are averaged over successful tasks in available logs; CTS improves/ties/regresses 5/4/0 apps with 17.8% average swap rate. Variant Isolated change SR vs base Avg solve steps Gemma-4 base no RL, greedy rollout Vanilla GRPO scalar comparative-judge reward CLIFT CLIFT +CTS certified step reward + URL advantages add conservative trajectory selection 61.8 64.7 72.6 74.6 Opus 4.6 closed-model reference, corrected common task IDs 69. +2.9 +10.8 +12.8 +8.0 15.4 18.5 16.0 15.5 Table 6 consolidates the ablations. Base Gemma-4 is the no-RL reference; vanilla GRPO isolates scalar judge-reward training; CLIFT adds certified step feedback; and CLIFT +CTS adds only testtime selection. Training accounts for most of the WAI gain, while CTS improves five apps, ties four, and never lowers the single-rollout CLIFT anchor. The decomposition further shows that the gain is not explained simply by additional interaction or inference-time search. Vanilla GRPO improves the base model by only 2.9 points while increasing the average number of steps on successful trajectories from 15.4 to 18.5. In contrast, CLIFT reaches 10.8-point improvement with an average of 16.0 steps, suggesting that the certified URL-local feedback primarily improves credit assignment rather than encouraging longer trajectories. CTS then adds further 2.0 points while reducing the average to 15.5 steps. Together with its 17.8% swap rate and zero per-app regressions, this supports the intended division of labor: CLIFT produces the stronger policy during training, while CTS intervenes selectively at test time when the certified bank provides sufficient evidence to prefer an alternative rollout.

sections.title: 5 Discussion and future work
sections.content: CLIFTs failures are intended to be visible. On WAI and VWA, many URL states accumulate enough observations for signed trust weights; on OM2W, the noisier live-web judge leaves more questions uncertified. This refusal is diagnostic rather than silent collapse: it says the current judge, state partition, or question bank does not support reliable distillation, and keeps noisy verifier evidence out of both the training reward and the CTS selector. The study is still bounded. We train one open-weight backbone and rely on frontier judge during training and bank construction; if that judge is systematically biased, calibration can detect disagreement only through observed data. The transfer results show that the bank can help stronger closed-source agents, but not that one bank is universal across all web domains. Stronger open web agents also carry misuse risk, so deployment should retain rate limits and domain-specific safeguards. 8 natural next step is to replace natural-language questions with executable browser-state assertions written by coding agent. The agent would learn not only to act on the web, but also to write compact checks that can be executed during rollouts and reused for test-time selection, reducing dependence on separate self-verification bank while preserving auditability.

sections.title: 6 Related work
sections.content: CLIFT sits at the intersection of web-agent benchmarks, RL credit assignment, test-time search, and reliable verifier-based selection. The closest systems usually improve one component of this loop: stronger web interfaces for agents, denser reward signals for training, or calibrated decision rules for deployment. CLIFT instead studies how one certified verification bank can connect these components, carrying judge feedback from online RL into test-time trajectory selection. Web agents and test-time search. Language agents combine reasoning, browser actions, and tools [Nakano et al., 2021, Yao et al., 2023b, Shinn et al., 2023, Schick et al., 2023, Qin et al., 2024]; search methods add deliberation or tree expansion at inference time [Wei et al., 2022, Yao et al., 2023a, Zhou et al., 2024a, Snell et al., 2025, Song et al., 2024]; and modern web, software, desktop, and embodied benchmarks stress realistic interfaces [Zhou et al., 2024b, Koh et al., 2024, Deng et al., 2023, Yao et al., 2022, Shridhar et al., 2021, Yang et al., 2024, Xie et al., 2024]. CLIFT differs from prompt-level search because its selector reuses certified per-URL bank learned during RL training, not just more samples. RL credit assignment and process rewards. GRPO and related RLVR methods improve LLMs from scalar outcomes [Schulman et al., 2017, Shao et al., 2024, DeepSeek-AI, 2025, Qi et al., 2025], while agent variants refine credit assignment through stratification, anchor states, success rates, or Monte-Carlo values [Zhu et al., 2025, Feng et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2025, Kazemnejad et al., 2025]. Process-verifier and rich-feedback methods provide denser supervision [Cobbe et al., 2021, Lightman et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2024, Hübotter et al., 2026, Madaan et al., 2023, Agarwal et al., 2024], and LLM judges provide it for open-ended generations [Bai et al., 2022, Liu et al., 2023, Zheng et al., 2023, Rafailov et al., 2023]. CLIFT keeps GRPO but changes the reward object: judge feedback is augmented by certified self-verifier and normalised by URL state. Conformal reliability and specification mining. Conformal prediction gives finite-sample reliability guarantees [Vovk et al., 2005, Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021, Gibbs and Candès, 2021, Vovk, 2012], with recent adaptations to language modeling, decision making, off-policy prediction, LLM-agent routing, and LLM judging [Quach et al., 2024, Lekeufack et al., 2024, Kuipers et al., 2024, Si et al., 2026, Badshah et al., 2026]. Those works calibrate outputs, policies, or judgments; CLIFT calibrates the verification questions themselves, using URL scope, polarity, and Mondrian-ACI trust weight. CEGAR-style loop [Clarke et al., 2000] turns judge rationales into reusable specifications for both training and test-time selection.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: CLIFT turns expensive judge feedback into reusable verifier for web agents: conformally certified URL-state evidence densifies training reward, then the frozen bank supports judge-free Conformal Trajectory Selection. Across WAI, VWA, and OM2W, the same bank helps train an open model, transfers to stronger closed model, and recalibrates for live-web selection without policy fine-tuning. trajectory score is consumed once; certified bank can be inspected, recalibrated, and reused. The bank is the durable artefact behind all three results. Each certified question carries URL scope, polarity sign, and trust weight derived from observed lift, with provenance back to the judge rationale that introduced it. This makes the bank small enough to ship with the agent, auditable when result looks off, and recoverable: when questions lift collapses on new distribution, the certifier withholds trust rather than amplifying noise. Together these properties give one knob, namely what the judge taught the agent to notice, that persists from training reward to test-time selection, from open backbone to closed backbone, and from sandboxed verifiers to live-web judges, and that stronger future judges can grow without discarding what earlier rounds taught.

sections.title: A Appendix
sections.content: This appendix contains evaluation prompts, the CLIFT-only training setup, detailed bank-transfer accounting for OM2W, and case studies drawn from evaluation logs. 12 A.1 Evaluation Prompts WAI browser-use agent prompt. The WAI browser-use rollout code uses the following system and user templates (abridged only by replacing runtime fields with braces). You are browsing agent completing task on web app. Each turn you see simplified accessibility snapshot of the current page listing interactable elements with numeric ids. turn: click(element_id), type_text(element_id, text, press_enter=True), scroll(direction), goto(url), go_back(), press(key), hover(element_id), stop(answer). Do not narrate. Task: {intent} Current URL: {url} Page title: {title} Accessibility snapshot: {snapshot} Recent action history: {history} Emit single tool call. Call exactly ONE tool per VWA Gemma-4 agent prompt. The VWA evaluation harness uses the Gemma-4 browser prompt below. You are an autonomous intelligent agent tasked with navigating web browser. You will be given web-based tasks. The users objective: This is the task youre trying to complete. The current web page screenshot has numbered interactable elements. The observation lists interactable elements as [id] [tagType] [text]. Use browser control tools to navigate and interact with pages. Rules: issue only valid actions; issue one tool call at time; reason step by step before acting; use element ids; verify before stop; do not stop prematurely; do not construct internal URLs with goto. OBJECTIVE: {objective} URL: {url} OBSERVATION: {observation} PREVIOUS ACTION: {previous_action} OM2W agent and WebJudge prompts. The OM2W rollout prompt uses the same browser-agent pattern, but for live websites and final-answer tasks: You are web browsing agent. You will be given task objective and must interact with real website to complete it. Each turn you receive screenshot with numbered element IDs, an accessibility tree, the current URL, and your previous action. Call exactly one tool per turn. Do not construct URLs; click links on the page. Never stop on the first step. to the relevant page first. Verify before calling stop. OBSERVATION: {observation} URL: {url} OBJECTIVE: {objective} PREVIOUS ACTION: {previous_action} For find/show/look-up tasks, navigate The canonical OM2W judge (WebJudge; Xue et al., 2025) first extracts key points, scores snapshots, and then applies the final judging prompt: You are an expert in evaluating the performance of web navigation agent. Given the users task, the agents action history, key points for task completion, and important web pages in the trajectory, determine whether the agent completed the task and achieved all requirements. Important criteria: match; submission/display actions must be completed; invalid or empty retrieved information may still be success if the required action was correctly performed. Respond in two lines: Thoughts: {reasoning} Status: "success" or "failure" filters must be applied correctly; exact ranges must 13 A.2 CLIFT Training Setup This subsection documents the training setup for the reported CLIFT checkpoint, organised into the four moving parts of the system: the backbone and the task pool that drives RL rollouts; the compute budget and shard layout; the per-rollout reward and verification loop; and the certification rule that turns the running bank into the deployment object loaded by CTS at test time. The concrete hyperparameter values used by all four stages are listed separately in A.3. Backbone and shard layout. The reported CLIFT checkpoint trains Gemma-4-31B-it with rank-8 LoRA adapter. We use 16 single-node shards, each with its own browser workers, reward pipeline, and LoRA adapter. After training, the per-shard adapters are averaged element-wise and merged into the base model for evaluation. OM2W is excluded from policy training entirely; we use it only for bank transfer and CTS at evaluation. Seed pool. The training pool is synthesised from scratch without reading any evaluation task. WAI seeds (186 tasks) are drawn from each applications schema and user-facing documentation; VWA seeds (206 tasks) come from separate SynthAgent crawl that probes the three Docker environments via header-only navigation. Both seed sets describe what the apps can do, not what the public benchmarks ask the agent to do. Frontier-LLM expansion. Two frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.5) expand each seed into draft pool of roughly 20 candidates per seed. Each expansion call sees only the seeds schema or crawl trace and small list of formatting constraints; it never sees the public benchmark task list, evaluator code, or any reference answer. Four-stage filter. shared filter then removes (i) malformed tasks that fail to parse or execute against sandbox replay, (ii) near duplicates under embedding-based dedup at cosine 0.92, (iii) hardcoded tasks whose answers are already present verbatim in the seed schema, and (iv) trivial-navigation tasks that resolve in single URL change without any UI interaction or form input. What remains is the 1,886 WAI and 1,272 VWA training tasks used for all reported runs. Train/eval isolation. At no point during synthesis, filtering, sharding, or RL training did the pipeline read WAI, VWA, or OM2W evaluation task descriptions, evaluation HTML/DOM snapshots, or evaluation reward signals. The eval suites are first loaded only after all training runs and adapter averaging are complete, and only by the read-only evaluator. Compute resources. Training ran as shard-parallel single-node jobs on H200 machines; at peak we used eight nodes, each with 8H200 GPUs, and completed 16 shard jobs across the WAI and VWA training pools. Within each node, resources were split between vLLM serving, LoRA optimization, and browser-rollout processes. Closed-backbone VWA and OM2W evaluations used GPT-5.5 API inference for rollouts and CTS candidates, but did not fine-tune the closed model. Rollout and verification loop. Each prompt produces GRPO group of = 8 browser rollouts. One comparative batch judge call scores the group at step level and supplies reasoning for CEGAR. In parallel, the base Gemma-4 model answers verification questions with the LoRA adapter detached, so verifier answers come from the same backbone without using the trained task adapter. Certification, reward, and deployment object. For each question, CCC maintains global, host, and URL-path Mondrian-ACI trackers with target α = 0.10 and lift-based trust weights; certification uses nmin = 50 and liftmin = 0.02. Certified verifier evidence is added through the asymmetric per-step blend, so it can support the judge reward but cannot subtract from it. The resulting URLstratified returns are written to token advantages over tool-call spans, and the frozen certified bank is the deployment object reused by CTS at test time. A.3 Reported CLIFT Hyperparameters The method section uses symbolic quantities; the concrete values used for the reported runs are: judge threshold θj = 0.5; GRPO group size = 8; certification target α = 0.10; minimum certification 14 count nmin = 50; minimum lift liftmin = 0.02; CEGAR interval = 60 training steps; CEGAR batch size 3 to 5 questions; reward blend β = 0.15; return discount γ = 0.95; CTS vote count = 3 with self-verifier temperature 0.7; greedy incumbent temperature 0; diverse retry temperature 1.0; and seed-bank sizes 281 WAI questions and 89 VWA questions before filtering and certification. A.4 Bank Details and OM2W Transfer This appendix tracks the construction, certification, and transfer of the verification banks that drive both training and test-time selection. For each benchmark we report the seed bank size, the size of the candidate bank after CEGAR-driven growth across training shards, the certified subset retained by the conformal certifier, and (for OM2W only) the subset that survives filtering and rewriting for live-web reuse. The same bank object is read by the training reward (2.2) and by CTS at test time (2.3); the numbers below describe how that object grows and shrinks at each stage. WAI and VWA training banks. The WAI training bank starts with 281 seed verification questions derived from app schemas and user documentation; the VWA training bank starts with 89 seed questions from SynthAgent site exploration of the three Docker environments. Both banks grow through the CEGAR refinement loop, in which the judge proposes 3 to 5 new questions every =60 training steps targeting rollouts that the existing bank fails to discriminate, and shrink through certification: questions whose lift falls below 0.02 at all tiers, or whose polarity is contradicted by observed lift, are demoted to neutral or dropped. After cross-shard merging, the WAI candidate bank totals 992 unique questions, of which 44 retain non-zero trust weights at one or more URL tiers and form the certified WAI bank used by the training reward and by CTS at test time. The VWA candidate bank totals 1,565 unique questions with 21 certified at the end of training. The 36 WAI and 48 VWA questions reported in Table 7 are the portion of each bank that the filter/rewrite stage judged general enough to reuse on live-web OM2W: certified questions kept as-is (7 WAI, 10 VWA) plus rewritten variants of certified or promising uncertified questions (29 WAI, 38 VWA). The remainder stay in their original training banks because their URL patterns or DOM references are appor environment-specific and do not transfer. Representative certified questions. To make the bank concrete, we walk through six representative certified questions drawn from the merged WAI and VWA banks, using the same prompt-style format as the agent and judge templates above. Each block shows the question identifier, the URL pattern at which it applies (* = global; the bank also contains per-host and per-URL-path refinements such as *google.com* and *reddit.com/r/* that share the same text but track separately under Mondrian-ACI), the observed trust weight (signed by polarity, magnitude scaled by lift), and the number of judge-scored observations that supported certification, followed by the YES/NO question that is asked of every rollout at runtime. Q.1: Reaching content-bearing pages (WAI, w=+0.54). The single strongest signal in the bank. Rollouts that visit page containing task-relevant content are far more likely to receive high judge score than rollouts that loiter on app homepages or navigation menus, and this pattern holds across all 9 WAI apps. * Identifier: made_meaningful_progress_toward_goal URL pattern: Trust weight: = +0.54, observations: = 82. Did the agent reach at least one page or state that contains information directly relevant to answering or completing the task (not just the app homepage or navigation menus)? 15 Q.2: Constructive non-destructive behaviour (WAI, w=+0.54). two-part check that distinguishes "did nothing harmful" from "did something productive". Rollouts that take destructive shortcuts (delete, cancel, revoke) without constructive counterpart fail this question even when the final URL looks plausible. * Identifier: avoided_destructive_unintended_actions URL pattern: Trust weight: = +0.54, observations: = 82. Did the agent both (a) avoid performing destructive actions (delete, cancel, revoke) not required by the task AND (b) take at least one constructive action toward the task goal? Q.3: Source-grounded final answer (WAI, w=+0.27). Targets common failure mode in information-retrieval tasks: emitting an answer without ever opening the page that actually contains the requested fact. Certified at high n, so the verifier has stable evidence at the global tier. * Identifier: extracted_info_from_correct_page URL pattern: Trust weight: = +0.27, observations: = 520. For information-retrieval tasks, did the agent extract its final answer from the page that actually contains the requested information? Q.4: End-state coherence (WAI, w=+0.26). simple URL coherence check that catches "wandered off" rollouts in which the agent ends on an unrelated section of the app. Cheap to answer for the base verifier (it only needs the final URL and the task description) and stable across apps. * Identifier: final_page_matches_task_context URL pattern: Trust weight: = +0.26, observations: = 238. Is the final URL or page the agent ended on relevant to the task objective rather than an unrelated section of the app? Q.5: Active search behaviour (VWA, w=+0.20). VWA-specific predicate. Distinguishes agents that submit query and then act on the results from agents that issue search and freeze on the results page without clicking through. Especially discriminative on the Classifieds and Shopping environments. * Identifier: used_search_and_acted_on_results URL pattern: Trust weight: = +0.20, observations: = 66. Did the agent both submit search query AND subsequently take meaningful action on the results (e.g., clicking result link rather than just observing the search page)? Q.6: Navigation depth (VWA, w=+0.13). Many VWA tasks require going past the search-results page to specific listing or product detail page to extract price, image, or description. This question rewards depth of navigation rather than breadth and is the highest-trust VWA question whose URL pattern is already general enough to translate to live-web OM2W without rewriting. * Identifier: visited_target_detail_page URL pattern: Trust weight: = +0.13, observations: = 200. Did the agent navigate to specific item detail page (product page, listing page, or submission page) relevant to the task, beyond the search results page? These six illustrate three properties the certifier rewards: the question must discriminate between highand low-judge rollouts (positive lift), it must be answerable from the trajectory by the base self-verifier (not too low-level for the LoRA-detached Gemma-4 to read off), and its YES/NO must align with the judges separation under the chosen polarity. Questions that fail these tests, e.g., ones that ask about UI elements specific to single page or that the base model cannot reliably answer, are demoted to neutral or dropped by the polarity-veto rule of Eq. 5. 16 Table 7: OM2W bank construction and recalibration. Questions come from WAI/VWA banks plus an OM2W-specific failure-mode expansion. Canonical judge is WebJudge [Xue et al., 2025] + o4-mini at threshold 4; Sonnet is cross-check. System Canonical SR Gain Sonnet SR Gemma-4 base Gemma-4 + ours GPT-5.5 low base GPT-5.5 high base GPT-5.5 high + ours GPT-5.5 high + ours 1 2 1 1 2 40.0 45.0 43.7 49.7 57.3 61.0 +5.0 +7.7 +11.3 46.8 partial positive 47.3 52.0 55.7 61.7 OM2W transfer setting. The main text reports the compact bank-transfer table. Here we keep the more detailed accounting for how the OM2W bank was produced and why it is strict transfer setting. No reported policy is trained on OM2W; only the question bank is filtered, rewritten, expanded, and recalibrated. Transferred question taxonomy. The filter/rewrite stage keeps general web-interaction predicates where possible and removes benchmark-specific app names or URL patterns when they do not transfer. The expansion stage adds questions for live-web failure modes observed on OM2W, including botblock pages, timeout or wandering behaviour, hallucinated extraction, partial-filter application, search-vs-detail-page confusion, and wrong-final-answer stops. The resulting 132-question bank uses the same schema as the training-time bank, so CTS loads it without code changes. Recalibration. Each question is scored on stratified pass/fail rollout sample using the base Gemma-4 verifier with logprob-extracted YES probabilities. Lift is computed as the pass/fail separation of the YES probability. Questions whose absolute lift is below the discrimination floor remain in the bank with zero weight; they can be re-certified later on different rollout sample. Among the 100 certified OM2W questions, 75 have positive lift and 25 have negative lift, so the selector receives both progress evidence and failure-mode evidence. A.5 OM2W Transfer Performance Details Table 8 reports the detailed cross-judge performance numbers behind the compact main-text OM2W figure. It is intentionally separate from Table 7: the bank table explains how the question set was transferred and recalibrated, while this table measures how much realised success that transferred evidence adds after CTS selects one trajectory to emit.
